items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Inline python -c one-liners use single-letter names in the core logic: `d=open(...)`, `c=sqlite3.connect`, `r=[...for i,n,v in ...]`. The final message explains the approach, but nothing in the code does.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No scratch-file clutter and no dead code. But decryption and extraction exist only as throwaway shell one-liners, not the small re-runnable decrypt/extract scripts the conventions asked for.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The key is hardcoded as `b^0x42` and never derived from the header in code. The script never checks the magic after XOR before overwriting the WAL, and has no error handling. Nothing is swallowed and it uses safe cp backups first.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The key came from evidence: long 0x4242 runs where zero bytes belong. After decrypting the whole file, xxd showed valid magic 0x377f0682. SQLite replayed the WAL itself, and the agent checked the result: `print(len(r))` gave 11 rows. No integrity_check, a minor gap.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: `cp main.db-wal /tmp/wal.bak && cp main.db /tmp/main.db.bak` ran before the in-place XOR and before any read-write SQLite open, which checkpointed and deleted the WAL.
